## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">About me
• 2007 to Present: Center for Assessment
 • Developed Student Growth Percentiles (SGP) and worked with over two
 dozen states on leveraging their longitudinal data systems
 • With the pandemic, tried to help states that I work with utilize the data
 they have to better communicate what has happened/is happening to
 students.
• 2004 to 2017: Assistant Professor at Boston College
• 1995 to 2004: University of Colorado, Boulder — Ph.D and Post-Doc
• 1989 to 2005: University of Wyoming — Ph.D Mathematics</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">COVID-19 Pandemic
• The COVID-19 Pandemic led to, arguably, the largest educational disruption in
 the history of the United States.
• Nearly 3 years into the pandemic and the impacts of the pandemic are still
 being felt.
• The pandemic impacted students academically, emotionally, physically, and
 financially.
• In this overview, we discuss three things:
 • Academic Impact: What is it and what happened to students.
 • Academic Recovery: What is it and what is happening.
 • Now What?: How can impact and recovery data be leveraged to help
 students going forward? Evidence-based investigations of what is working.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">What is Academic Impact?
What is Academic Recovery?
• The pandemic and all the ensuing disruptions functioned/functions
 as an academic headwind, impeding (in general) the academic
 progress of students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
 ▪ They slow one’s rate of progress (speedometer)
 ▪ And by slowing one’s rate of progress they lead to less distance being travelled
 (odometer).
• In education odometer is to attainment as speedometer is to growth.
• Academic impact is analogous to a headwind, decreasing the rate of
 student learning (deceleration) which, in turn leads to lower
 attainment
 5</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">What is Academic Impact?
What is Academic Recovery?
• Academic recovery is analogous to an academic tailwind,
 increasing the rate of student learning (acceleration) which, in
 turn leads to higher attainment.
• During Fall 2021 to present, under the presumption that student
 education got back to normal, the hope was that rates of learning
 stabilized to pre-pandemic rates or, even better, increased to rates
 exceeding pre-pandemic rates allowing students to catch-up.
• Examination of academic impact/recovery are opposite sides of
 the same coin and utilize the same analytics.

 6</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Impact &amp; Recovery
• We investigate impact/recovery in two ways:
 • Change in same grade/same cohort attainment: We examine equi-percentile
 change in attainment. Impact: 2019 to 2021, Recovery 2021 to 2022
 • Change in student growth: We examine change in baseline (pre-pandemic)
 student growth (SGPs). Impact: 2019 to 2021 (using 2017 to 2019 growth
 norms), Recovery: 2021 to 2022 (using 2018 to 2019 growth norms).</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/08.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Assessment Data
• We investigated the impacts in achievement and growth of the pandemic
 across two time frames:
 • Impact: Spring 2020 through Summer 2021
 • Recovery: Fall 2021 through Summer 2022
• To investigate impact we utilized two primary sources of data
 • State summative assessment data
 • Impact: State summative assessment Spring 2019 to Spring 2021
 • Recovery: State summative Spring 2021 to Spring 2022
 • State English Language Proficiency Data (ACCESS)
 • Impact: ACCESS Winter 2020 to Winter 2021
 • Recovery: ACCESS Winter 2021 to Winter 2022

 8</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Assessment Data
• Other sources of data exists to investigate these phenomena
 • Interim assessment
 • NAEP
• I have looked at state summative, interim and NAEP and the untidy reality is
 that:
 • Big picture: They broadly tell the same thing (e.g., bigger impacts in math
 than in ELA)
 • When you look more closely, they can tell different stories
• Different assessment can tell different things, even if the same methodology
 is used on those data sets.
• State assessment data is in my opinion the highest quality data being used
 right now.

 9</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/11.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Impact Analyses
• Worked with 12 states to analyses their data to determine academic
 impact in 2021
• State summative tests were cancelled in 2020 so analyses of state
 summative tests were done from 2019 to 2021
• ELP assessments (WIDA-ACCESS) were not cancelled so analyzed
 data from 2020 to 2021

 11</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/13.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Summary
We summarize the academic impact both
overall and by achievement quintile
For Grade 8 mathematics, the overall
academic impact for students was large (z
decrease = -0.29 and median SGP decrease =
-22)
Academic impact was not uniform across
students. For this grade/content area higher
achieving students were more severely
impacted than lower achieving student.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/19.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Phase
• During the 2021-2022 academic year, school returned to normal for most
 students.
• The hope was that a return to normal would lead recovery of the academic losses
 incurred by students.
• Because learning slowed during the initial phase of the pandemic, to make up for
 those losses, learning must accelerate to rates above normal in order to catch-up
 for those loses.
• Data from two sources was utilized to examine whether recovery is occurring:
 • State summative data from 2021 and 2022
 • WIDA-ACCESS data from 2021 and 2022</div>
```
